newsitem.title: CENTRAL AFRICAN REPUBLIC: Central African Rep announces unity government.
newsitem.headline: Central African Rep announces unity government.

text.p: Central African Republic announced the formation of a national unity government on Tuesday to try to end a cycle of ethnic violence provoked by three bloody army mutinies.
Under an African-mediated deal, the new 28-member government, led by outgoing foreign minister Michel Gbezera-Bria, includes members of 10 political parties plus members from society at large.
But the main portfolios went to supporters of President Ange-Felix Patasse, either from his own Movement for the Liberation of the Centralafrican People (MLPC) or allied parties.
They include Doctor Pascal Kado, who takes charge of defence and restructing the army -- a key task after the army mutinies.
The head of Patasse's presidential guard, General Francois Djader Bedaya, takes the key post of territorial administration and public security -- the equivalent of interior minister.

Outgoing defence minister Jean-Mette Yapende takes over foreign affairs while fellow Patasse supporters Anicet Georges Dologuele and Christophe Mbremaidou take the finance and budget portfolio and the economic reform, planning, international cooperation portfolio respectively.
Presidential spokesman Prospere Ndouba announced the new government on state television in a presidential decree.
Patasse named Gbezera-Bria on January 30 to head the new government. Tuesday's announcement followed more than two weeks of tortuous negotiations which at one stage looked in danger of collapsing.
Mali's widely respected former military leader Amadou Toumani Toure brokered the January 25 Bangui Accords.
Mutinies in April and May began over pay and conditions but turned into a campaign to oust Patasse, a northern civilian who won presidential elections in 1993.
The latest mutiny, which began on November 15, degenerated into ethnic feuding. The mutineers were from the minority Yakoma tribe of former military leader Andre Kolingba.
French troops, in the country under a defence pact, stepped in to restore order. Estimates of those killed in the mutinies range from scores to several hundred.

Troops from Mali, Burkina Faso, Gabon and Chad, whose presidents launched the mediation effort in December at the behest of a Franco-African summit, are taking over from French troops who have been keeping rival factions apart.
Troops from Senegal and Togo are also part of this force.
The Central African country hit world headlines during the extravagant reign of Jean-Bedel Bokassa, who was toppled in a French-backed coup in 1979.
